headline: SAME AREA. SAME FRICTION?
body: Equal area does not establish equal friction.
slides.alt: Real ductwork provides context for the question of equal area and friction; no pressure-loss measurement is shown.

headline: TWO SECTIONS. ONE AREA.
body: Illustrative clear internal dimensions.

headline: SAME FLOW. SAME MEAN VELOCITY.
body: Both areas are 1 ft^2.
At the same volume-flow reference basis,
V = Q / A gives the same mean velocity.
slides.alt: Two equal-area duct sections with equal illustrative flow and cross-sectional mean velocity; same reference basis.

headline: THE GEOMETRY CHANGES.
body: Perimeter: 48 in versus 60 in.
Area alone does not describe wetted perimeter.
This is not a pressure-loss ratio.
slides.alt: Original section outlines highlight perimeter48inches for12by12and60inches for6by24; no friction ratio claimed.

headline: CHECK THE FRICTION METHOD.
body: Rectangular friction equivalence needs more than area.
Length, roughness and fittings still matter.
Hydraulic diameter is not equivalent round diameter.
slides.alt: Geometry-aware comparison reminder; hydraulic diameter is explicitly distinguished from friction-equivalent round diameter.

headline: LOWER RH. LESS MOISTURE?
body: Not necessarily.
Relative humidity and humidity ratio
answer different questions.
slides.alt: Contextual air-handler photograph introduces the difference between relative humidity and moisture content.

headline: TWO DIFFERENT MEASURES.
body: RH: vapor pressure / saturation vapor pressure
at that temperature.
Humidity ratio: water-vapor mass / dry-air mass.
slides.alt: Two separate definitions: relative humidity as a vapor-pressure ratio and humidity ratio as water-vapor mass per dry-air mass.

headline: WARM THE SAME AIR.
body: Heating only. Fixed total pressure.
No moisture added or removed.
Humidity ratio stays constant.
slides.alt: Original conceptual heating path with fixed total pressure and no moisture exchange; humidity ratio stays constant.

headline: RH CAN FALL.
body: Saturation vapor pressure increases as temperature rises.
RH falls in this heating-only example.
Water-vapor content has not decreased.
slides.alt: A conceptual temperature rise and relative-humidity decrease with unchanged humidity ratio; no numerical equipment performance asserted.

headline: DEHUMIDIFICATION IS DIFFERENT.
body: Removing moisture lowers humidity ratio.
Lower RH alone does not prove moisture removal.
Concept only, not equipment diagnosis.
slides.alt: Conceptual comparison separates moisture removal from heating-only relative-humidity change.
